title: Design Memory Allocator
statement:
Design a class `Allocator` that manages a row of `n` memory cells, numbered `0` to `n - 1`. At the start every cell is free.

- `Allocator(n)` sets up the `n` free cells.
- `allocate(size, mID)` looks for a run of `size` free cells that sit next to each other, choosing the run with the smallest starting index. If one exists, all its cells are marked as owned by `mID` and its starting index is returned; otherwise nothing changes and `-1` is returned.
- `freeMemory(mID)` makes every cell owned by `mID` free again and returns how many cells that was (`0` if there were none).

The same `mID` may own several separate runs, and `freeMemory` releases all of them at once.
constraints: At most 1000 calls in total are made to allocate and freeMemory
notes:
## Intuition

With at most 1000 cells and 1000 calls, the memory can simply be modelled as an array where each cell holds its owner's `mID`, or `0` when free (ids start at 1, so `0` never clashes). A brute-force check of every possible starting index and every block works too, but one left-to-right pass that counts the current stretch of free cells finds the leftmost fitting run directly: the first time the stretch reaches `size`, it ends at the current index.

## Approach

1. The constructor creates `memory`, an array of `n` zeros.
2. `allocate(size, mID)`: walk `i` from left to right, keeping `run`, the number of free cells ending at `i`. A free cell extends it; an owned cell resets it to 0.
3. As soon as `run === size`, the run spans `start = i - size + 1` to `i`. Write `mID` into those cells and return `start`.
4. If the walk ends without that happening, return `-1`.
5. `freeMemory(mID)`: scan every cell; each one holding `mID` becomes 0 and adds one to `freed`. Return `freed`.

## Example 1, step by step

`memory` starts as ten zeros. The three `allocate(1, ·)` calls each stop at the first free cell, giving `0`, `1`, `2`. `freeMemory(2)` clears cell 1 and returns `1`. `allocate(3, 4)` sees `run = 1` at cell 1, a reset at cell 2, then `run` reaches 3 at cell 5, so `start = 3`. The next `allocate(1, 1)` fills cell 1, and the one after fills cell 6. `freeMemory(1)` clears cells 0, 1 and 6 and returns `3`. `allocate(10, 2)` never reaches a run of 10, so it returns `-1`, and `freeMemory(7)` finds nothing and returns `0`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) per call: each method scans the array once (the fill touches at most `size` cells).
- Space: O(n) for `memory`.

## Pitfalls

- Reset `run` on every owned cell; a run must be made of neighbouring free cells.
- The start of the run is `i - size + 1`, not `i - size`.
- `freeMemory` must release every block of that `mID`, not just the first one, and return the total number of cells.
- A failed `allocate` must leave memory untouched, so write only after a full run is found.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `memory` | owner of each cell, `0` when free |
| `run` | number of consecutive free cells ending at `i` |
| `start` | first index of the run being allocated |
| `i`, `j` | scan index and fill index |
| `freed` | number of cells released by `freeMemory` |
